lesson.title: Whiskers That Stop Short: Building the Modified Boxplot
lesson.summary: See how the modified boxplot uses the 1.5 times IQR rule to stop its whiskers at real data values and plot outliers separately, giving a more honest picture than an ordinary boxplot.
lesson.body:
A basic boxplot draws its whiskers all the way out to the minimum and the maximum of the data set, which means a single freakishly large or small value can stretch one whisker far past where the bulk of the data actually lives. That single long whisker quietly hides the fact that one point is fundamentally different from the rest. The modified boxplot fixes this by refusing to let the whiskers run all the way to values that the 1.5 times IQR rule has flagged as outliers.

Building a modified boxplot starts the same way as an ordinary boxplot: find the five-number summary, minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum, draw a box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, and mark the fences at Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR and Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR. The difference comes next. Instead of extending each whisker all the way to the minimum and maximum, you extend it only to the most extreme data value that still falls inside the fences. Any point beyond a fence is plotted as its own dot, asterisk, or other individual symbol, separated from the whisker entirely.

Return to the push-up data: 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24, 25, 40. The five-number summary is minimum 12, Q1 = 15, median = 19, Q3 = 24, maximum 40, and the earlier fence calculation gave a lower fence of 1.5 and an upper fence of 37.5. The box runs from 15 to 24 with a line at 19. On the low end, 12 is inside the fence of 1.5, so the lower whisker extends down to 12, the true minimum. On the high end, 40 is outside the fence of 37.5, so the upper whisker cannot reach it, instead it extends only to 25, the largest value still within the fence, and 40 is plotted as an isolated point beyond the whisker.

Looking at the finished graph, you can read off almost everything important in one glance: the middle 50 percent of students did between 15 and 24 push-ups, the typical student did about 19, the data are only mildly stretched toward high values among the non-outliers, and there is one student whose performance is disconnected from the rest of the group. None of that nuance survives in an ordinary boxplot, where the top whisker would stretch all the way to 40 and visually suggest a smooth, gradual increase in performance rather than one dramatic jump.

This is exactly why the modified boxplot depends on identifying outliers first. Without the 1.5 times IQR rule telling you where the fences are, you would not know where to stop the whisker or which points to plot separately. The modified boxplot is really just the ordinary boxplot with the outlier rule layered on top, which is why AP Statistics treats it as the default boxplot to draw and interpret in almost every practical situation.

Modified boxplots also shine when you place several of them side by side to compare groups, since an outlier in one group will not distort the visual comparison of medians and spreads the way it would if every whisker had to reach the extreme values. A coach comparing push-up counts across three gym classes can see at a glance which class has the highest median, which has the most spread, and which has an unusual individual, all without the outlier dragging one whisker off the chart.
